title: From Vaudeville to the Subway: How a Brooklyn Station Became a Kaleidoscopic Stage
summary: Most New Yorkers associate theater with Broadway's glittering marquees, but deep in Brooklyn, a subway station now holds its own spectacular stage. At the Church Avenue stop, artist Christopher Myers has installed four kaleidoscopic glass-tiled panels that celebrate Flatbush's rich but often overlooked performing arts legacy. The mosaics, unveiled in March, are titled "If you don't want your children to know the truth about life don't send 'em to the theater." Each day, over 10,000 commuters encounter the vibrant scenes, which Myers spent three months researching. He unearthed a turn-of-the-century vaudeville scene and the Afro-Caribbean migration that brought carnival traditions like stilt walking to Brooklyn's West Indian Day Parade. The panels feature six figures, with the most prominent being Moms Mobley—the stage name of pioneering Black comedian Loretta Mary Aiken. She's depicted mid-act, in front of a red velvet curtain bedazzled with stars and a giant hand, a nod to a Hungarian immigrant artist who painted many of the city's theaters. Myers, a Queens-born artist whose work has appeared in the Guggenheim, calls the subway "the most democratic space I will ever get to share my work." He's seen kids at the station, curious about the characters. The installation is part of the MTA's Arts & Design program, which sets aside one percent of renovation budgets for permanent art. The competition was fierce: 306 artists submitted proposals, and Myers was one of four finalists. Tina Vaz, the program's director, said the panel was impressed by his deep research and how the work "interrupts the ordinary with moments of pause, connections, and beauty." The mosaics took 13 months to fabricate in Mexico and two weeks to install. Now, Myers joins the ranks of public art legends like Roy Lichtenstein and Yoko Ono. The experience has inspired him to create more mosaics for institutions across the country, but he remains viscerally connected to the subway where he first encountered art as a kid riding from LeFrak City. "New York is the only 24-hour subway system," he said. "It's so much a part of our everyday life."
why_it_matters: Public art like this shows that creativity isn't locked away in expensive museums—it can surprise you on your daily route and make a commute feel like a story about your own neighborhood's past and future.

background_read: Christopher Myers (a Queens-born artist who has shown work in the famous Guggenheim Museum) is part of a long tradition of public art in New York's transit system. The MTA's Arts & Design program, started in the 1980s, sets aside one percent of station renovation budgets for permanent works by artists, leading to over 300 installations across the city.

Flatbush, the Brooklyn neighborhood around the Church Avenue station, has deep roots in both vaudeville-era entertainment and later waves of Afro-Caribbean immigration. By the early 1900s, performers from all backgrounds filled local music halls; after the 1960s, Caribbean carnival customs—especially from Trinidad and Jamaica—became a defining part of the area's culture.

Myers's research uncovered forgotten facts, such as the role of a Hungarian immigrant artist who painted theater interiors. His colorful panels function like a time machine, linking the neighborhood's past stages to today's daily subway ride.

perspectives.description: Commuters get a free, daily encounter with beauty that honors the area's forgotten cultural heroes, turning a routine subway stop into a source of local identity.
Some wonder if the one percent renovation budget spent on art could instead fund better infrastructure or cleaner stations, questioning whether aesthetics matter as much as function.
The panels function like a historical document, making visible how migration and entertainment shaped New York—an ongoing cycle where new communities bring new forms of performance to the city.

This installation could spark more artists to reinvent forgotten neighborhood stories, transforming transit systems nationwide into living museums that connect commuters to the places they rush through.
